9.23.12.en: * "Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours" (Mk 12:7). How foolish you are! How will the inheritance be yours? Is it because you killed him? Yes, you killed him, but the inheritance will not be yours... When you boasted that you had killed him, he had only fallen asleep, for he said in another psalm, "I laid me down and slept."

9.23.13.en: They plotted and wanted to kill me, and I slept; had I not willed it, I would not have slept.

9.23.14.en: I slept, for [I have power to lay down (my life), and I have power to take it again] (Jn 10:18).

9.23.15.en: [I laid me down and slept; I awaked] (Ps 3:5).

9.23.16.en: Rage, you Jews! Let the earth be given into the hands of the wicked, that is, let the body be left in the hands of the persecutors, that they may hang it on a tree, fasten it with nails, and pierce it with a spear.

9.23.17.en: Did not the One who sleeps add that He also rises?.. When was Eve created? When Adam slept! When did the sacraments of the Church come forth from the side of Christ? When He slept on the Cross.

9.23.18.en: * Let the persecutors rage! Let the earth be given into the hand of the wicked (Job 10:17)! Let the body be nailed to the tree with nails, and pierced with a spear. For He who lies down and sleeps says, [I shall rise again](ح).

9.24.s.en: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

9.24.0.en: 25 Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good. 26 They are passed away as the swift ships: as the eagle that hasteth to the prey. 27 If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness, and comfort myself: 28 I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent. 29 If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain? 30 If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean; 31 Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me.

9.24.1.en: "Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good" [25].

9.24.2.en: The speed of runners (who run before the chariot) was often used in ancient times to carry urgent messages. The kings kept some of these runners for the service of the royal palace.

9.24.3.en: When King Hezekiah sent an invitation to all Israel and Judah to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, "the posts went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah" (2 Chr 30:6). In the days of Jeremiah it seems that this service had become established and organized, for in his prophecy about the destruction of Babylon it was said: "One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the king of Babylon that his city is taken at one end" (Jer 51:31). The Persians likewise used swift messengers. They were used when the order was issued to kill all the Jews in the empire (Esth 3:13, 15), and also when the order was issued to take vengeance on their enemies: "So the posts that rode upon mules and camels went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment" (Esth 8:14).

9.24.4.en: * Tell me, what is steadfast in this world? Is it wealth, which often does not remain even until evening? Or is it glory? Listen to what a righteous man says: "My life is swifter than a runner."

9.24.5.en: St. John Chrysostom. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that God created man to see good, that is, to see God, the supreme Good. But once sin entered his life, he lost his inner sight and no longer beheld the divine light nor saw good, and so he doubts the dealings of God.

9.24.6.en: * Man was created for this purpose, to see good, which is God. But since he did not wish to stand in the light, he fled from the light and lost his eyes. On the same level he committed himself to bodily things through sin. So he became subject to blindness and unable to see the inner light...

9.24.7.en: But when we think about such matters, doubting continually (about God as the maker of good things), hard questions press upon us as we keep silent: "Why does God create a person whom He foresaw would perish? Why, being the greatest in power and goodness, did He not intend to create man unable to perish?"

9.24.8.en: And while the mind questions thus in its silence, man fears that in his rashness through these questions he will fall into pride, and so he draws back toward humility, which restrains the thoughts of the heart.

9.25.0.en: And the more he came into severe trials, in the midst of troubles, the more he suffered over the interpretation of the hidden meaning of events. Therefore he continues: [If I say, I will not speak in this way, I change the look of my face and am struck with grief] [27].

9.25.2.en: "They are passed away as the swift ships."

9.25.3.en: "As the eagle that hasteth to the prey" (his catch) [26].

9.25.4.en: The days of his prosperity have departed like a ship hastening to its safe harbor, and like the eagle that swoops down on its prey in the twinkling of an eye. As no trace remains of the ship after it has passed, nor of the eagle in the air after it has swooped on its prey, so the days of prosperity have passed and no trace of them is left. Behold, time hurries man as though to vanishing; soon it carries us over into eternity, and time will have no place in our eternity.

9.25.5.en: * "Our life is swifter than a runner; it passes and nothing is seen. It is like the passage of a ship, or like a flying eagle seeking food" (Job 9:25-26) LXX; so passes the life of man. What we say we forget, and no sign of our passing remains visible except that it is filled with sorrow and grief. "I am smitten in all my limbs. Is there a mediator between us, to reprove and decide between us?" (Job 9:28, 33) LXX.

9.25.6.en: St. Ambrose. * As the sea leaves no traces of ships, and there are no traces in the air of the eagle swooping on its prey (Wis 5:10-11), so it is with the wealth of the world when it passes: it will not leave a particle of the traces of happiness. For wealth and what comes from it is cast into oblivion. For this reason Job, as an example, despised every influence of that life and its instability, and he advises us not to be attached to it.

9.25.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness (my face), and comfort myself (and smile)" [27].

9.25.8.en: It seems that Job began to look beyond time and to find that his distress would one day be dissolved and cease to exist, when his soul departs from this world and all his life becomes like a shadow that has passed, leaving no trace. He said to himself that he would forget the distress he was in, leave his cares, and be comforted or rejoice (laugh).

9.25.9.en: Even if righteous Job wanted not to speak in the midst of his affliction, and resolved in his heart to ignore what had befallen him, the look on his face bears witness to the violence of the trial and speaks of the harshness and fury of the storm, without his uttering a word.

9.25.10.en: * The evils that come upon you will pass, and He whom you await with patience will come. He will wipe away the sweat of weariness. He will dry every tear, and there will be weeping no more. Here below we must groan in the midst of trials, as Job asks: [What is the life of man on earth but a trial?] (Job 7:1).

9.26.0.en: St. Augustine. "I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent" [28].

9.26.1.en: Job sees that if he were to enter even into a dialogue with himself about his sufferings, he might sin against God; therefore he fears to think about them, since he cannot be justified. He feared to reproach God for permitting him these sufferings, because he knows that by this God would not acquit him, but it would be against him.

9.26.2.en: * [I was afraid of all my works, knowing that you would not acquit me when I am guilty] [28-29].

9.26.3.en: What works the blessed Job practiced, this holy history has made plain. For he had learned to propitiate his Creator by offering many burnt offerings. According to the number of his sons, as it is written, he rose up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each one of them, cleansing them not only from unclean deeds but also from evil thoughts. He recorded for us, with the testimony of the Holy Bible: "For Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" (Job 1:5).

9.26.4.en: He practiced compassion, as he declared of himself when his friends troubled him: "Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?" (Job 30:25). He undertook the role of tenderness, for he says: "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" (Job 29:15).

9.26.5.en: He kept the purity of chastity in his heart; in this he reveals himself most clearly and with dignity: "If mine heart have been deceived by a woman" (Job 31:9).

9.26.6.en: He reached the highest summit of humility from the depths of his heart, for he says: [If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me] (Job 31:13).

9.26.7.en: He gave with great generosity, saying: "Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof?" (Job 31:17)... He practiced hospitality, saying: "The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller" (Job 31:32).

9.26.8.en: And in the midst of all these things, to complete his virtues by the highest way of love, he loved his very enemies. He says of this: "If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul" (Job 31:29-30).

9.26.9.en: Why then was the saint afraid of his works (Job 9:28), when he had always practiced works that make God yield before disobedience? How is this? How could he fear even these wonderful works in dread, saying: [I am afraid of all my works] [28]? Unless we conclude from the works and words of the saint that, if we truly wish to please God after overcoming evil habits, we must fear the very good works we practice. For there are especially two things that we must seriously dread in the practice of good works, namely: slackness and deceit. It was said by the prophet according to the old translation: [Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully and slackly] (Jer 48:10).

9.26.10.en: A man commits the crime of deceit in the work of the Lord when he loves himself excessively for the good works he has done, and exerts all his effort to turn good works into a reward. Likewise it is fitting for us to bear in mind that there are three ways in which deceit is practiced: its aim is either to win the secret feelings of one's fellow creatures, or to seek praise, or to obtain an external (material) benefit. In contrast, it was said by the prophet of the upright man: [Blessed is he that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes] (cf. Isa 33:15)... that is, if he does not aim at vainglory from his fellows, nor flattery from their lips, nor gifts from their hands...

9.26.11.en: For this reason, good works themselves cannot escape the sin that lurks in them unless they are guarded by great fear. Therefore the saint rightly said in this place: [I was afraid of all my works].

9.27.0.en: "If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain?" [29]

9.27.1.en: Job sees that he wearies himself in vain to be cleared before God.

9.27.2.en: * He who knows the weakness of human nature experiences the power of God.

9.27.3.en: Fr. Maximus the Confessor. * He says: I know that I am weak before the infinite justice of God; but before men I am righteous according to your testimony (Job 1:1, 8; 2:3).

9.27.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Because these men beheld the greatness of God, the smallness of their own persons appeared to them. They looked upon the waves of His splendor, the purity of His nature, the wonder of His eternity, the glory of His majesty, the power of His limitlessness, the sublime beauty of His holiness, and upon these things that exist naturally from Him, and upon Him, and for Him, and through Him. So their thoughts were enlightened to see their own souls and to contemplate their persons, as it is written. They were also on guard lest the answer of iniquity be found in their hearts, or the thought that leads to supposing that the goodness of their persons was merited by their virtues, so as to reach the summit of God's greatness.

9.27.5.en: * My soul cannot stand firm in true humility, see its own smallness, and consider the poverty of its nature, unless the hidden riches of God dazzle it and the loftiness of His sight moves it. Poverty is left behind through riches, and darkness is hated through the shining of light. And the humility of the soul is felt from the wondrous loftiness of God; he who has sensed the greatness of God sees his own smallness.

9.28.0.en: St. Jacob of Serugh. "If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean" [30].

9.28.1.en: * Snow is the tears of humility, in which all the other virtues are exalted in the eyes of the strict Judge... For some grieve, but not in humility; when they grieve they weep, yet they offer these very tears while despising the lives of their brethren, or in arrogance against the dispensation of their Creator. These have water but not snow water, and they cannot wash, because they do not wash with the tears of humility. But he who washes and is cleansed from sin by snow is the one who says in assurance: [A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise] (Ps 51:17).

9.28.2.en: * "Snow" can also be understood in another sense. Water comes from a spring and from a stream flowing out of the earth, but snow falls from heaven. Very many grieve, lamenting over earthly things... They wound themselves with pain in their prayers, but because of their joy in temporal pleasures they do not wash with snow, for their tears flow from below...

9.28.3.en: But those who grieve because they long for rewards on high are washed and cleansed with snow, for heavenly compunction overflows upon them. For they seek eternity with tears and sorrow, with longing for it kindled in them, and by this they receive from on high the means by which they are cleansed.

9.28.4.en: * What is meant by the hands but "works"? The prophet said to certain persons: [Your hands are full of blood] (Isa 1:15), meaning "your works are full of cruelty."

9.28.6.en: * In this great battle, since man lives under grace and it helps him, and therefore he fights well and rejoices in the Lord with fear, he does not need mighty fighters or fierce destroyers to put to death the deeds of the flesh; rather we can be healed of some wounds of sin by this daily saying: "And forgive us our debts" (Mt 6:12), striving with this prayer against the vices and against Satan, the chief of vice, with very great care and exceeding skill, nullifying his deadly counsels, which he offers, namely that man should not condemn himself and should offer excuses with which to justify his sins.

9.28.7.en: These (satanic) counsels not only leave the wounds unhealed, but drive them to grave and deadly harm.

9.28.8.en: And here appears the need for a chastity full of watchfulness, so as to restrain the lust of human pride, in which man is pleased with himself and does not wish to see in himself that he is worthy of blame. So when he sins he disdains to confess his sin, and instead of accusing himself with healing humility, he looks for an excuse to offer with deadly arrogance.

9.28.9.en: And to restrain this pride, we find him who asked chastity from God with the words "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Incline not my heart to any evil thing," fearing lest he "practise wicked works." For this "excusing" is more than evil speech..

9.28.10.en: For the wicked man denies that he is wicked, in spite of committing the evil that he cannot deny. Since he cannot hide the doing of evil, because it is plain that he has committed it, he looks for a way to ascribe the evil to another, thinking by this that he keeps himself far from what he deserves.

9.28.11.en: And since he does not wish in himself to be a criminal, he adds to his fault another fault by offering justifications. And instead of accusing himself of his sins, he offers excuses, not knowing that by this he removes from himself pardon, not punishment.

9.29.0.en: St. Augustine. "Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me" [31].

9.29.1.en: In ancient times it was thought that snow water had the property of cleansing the skin. They thought that the skin became white by means of snow water, and that it prevented sweat. And some thought that a black person could make his skin white by washing in snow.

9.29.2.en: There is no way to be acquitted before God: snow is unable to clean his skin, nor lye (soap or cleanser) his hands. There is no use in it, for the more man tries to clear himself, the more he finds himself plunged into the mire (the ditch), until he hates his clothes and loathes to touch himself.

9.29.3.en: Perhaps Job sees that not only is it vain to clear himself before those around him, but with every attempt at acquittal God uncovers his hidden weaknesses, and he sees himself sunk in the mire, loathsome in the sight of men. Job did not dare to dispute with God as though He were a man like himself, for the pot has no right to argue with the potter.

9.29.4.en: * It is clear that men are called righteous and are said to be without faults, but if negligence creeps in on them they fall. Man always occupies the middle place: he can slip from the height of virtue into vice, and he can rise from vice to virtue. He will not be safe, but must fear the wreck of his ship even in fair weather; therefore no man can be without sin. Solomon says: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20). Likewise in the book of Kings: "There is no man that sinneth not" (1 Kgs 8:46; 2 Chr 6:36). Likewise the blessed David says: [Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults. Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins] (Ps 19:12-13). And again: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). And the Holy Bible is full of such statements.

9.29.5.en: St. Jerome. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's words here the cries of repentance, for he feels that although he is righteous in the sight of men, he is guilty in the eyes of God, and so he asks for pardon. Thus Job lived all his life seeking repentance, and so his life became blessed.

9.29.6.en: * In one day, my brother, you can acquire all eternity, and in one day you can lose it. Thousands of days have been given to you on earth to be used for your eternal salvation or your eternal judgment. Blessed a hundred times is the day on which you repent of all your evil works and defiled words and thoughts, and return to God with a cry asking for mercy. This day is better for you than a thousand other days!

9.29.7.en: What is this blessed day? It is the day of man's condemnation of himself. When the dawn of that day breaks, the man who until then had condemned the whole world, when he looks at himself, sees that he is the greatest sinner on God's earth. He feels shame before God, before every man, and before everything that God has created on earth. This shame is kindled in him like a fire; then he knows and confesses: "I am the greatest sinner on God's earth, all other men are better than I... Lord, have mercy on me, Lord, I am the sinner, and wash me from the mire of my sins, that I may begin to be like Your creation."

9.29.8.en: Do not expect, my brother, that the blessed day of repentance will come of itself, but lay hold of it on the first day it meets you, and say: "You are the blessed day on which I buy eternal life."

9.29.9.en: Bishop Nikolai Velimirovich. * What is meant by "clothes" but the earthly body, in which the soul is wrapped and covered...? It is said that our clothes abhor us, since they make us hated. He who said: "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members" (Rom 7:23) felt the hatred of the clothes. These very clothes, in which he was never able to find final delight, he longed with all zeal to cast aside, that he might one day receive them back in a far better state, saying: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"

9.30.0.en: 32 For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment. 33 Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both. 34 Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me: 35 Then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me.

9.30.1.en: "For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment" [32].

9.30.2.en: * What does this mean, approximately? If the one who punishes me were a man, his punishments would not entirely condemn the one who falls under them. I could stand trial before him and prove to him that he is unjust, but because You are God, this is impossible.

9.31.0.en: St. John Chrysostom. "Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both!" [33]

9.31.1.en: Job's complaint represents the cry of humanity since its fall, for it is in need of a mediator to whom it can resort, to bring man back into the divine embrace. Who is the one who has the power to stretch out his hand in love to join man to God? Who has such boldness, except the Word of God incarnate, who is one with the Father in the same essence, and equal to Him, and who became one with the sons of men, becoming the second Adam?

9.31.2.en: Since our Lord Jesus Christ alone is the Intercessor without sin, He is able to do the work of reconciliation between the Father and man.

9.31.3.en: * Do you not see how Job proclaimed the coming of Christ, prophesying under the appearance of this prayer the mystery of the mediator of our life? For this reason Paul also said: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). For what would happen if Christ had become incarnate and repeated what Isaiah said in rebuking the people? "Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:16-18).

9.31.4.en: Why is Christ called "the Mediator"? Because He took the form of man and of God (Phil 2:6). It is necessary for the mediator to be able to lead enemies to reconciliation (Rom 5:10), to bear the face of both; for by this he achieves agreement and reconciliation. And since Christ wanted to reconcile man with his Father (2 Cor 5:18), being God and becoming man (Phil 2:7), He took the form of both.

9.31.5.en: Indeed He went further than this; for He declares to men what He does in the matter of their judgment, how He is the Judge and yet the One who loves them, and how the Judge appears as the doer of good and the compassionate; for He describes washing, bearing witness to the washing of Baptism.

9.31.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us with God through the sacrifice of His blood...

9.31.7.en: Christ came to destroy the enemies, to make peace, and to reconcile us with God, from whom we were separated by the barrier of evil that we erected by our sins.

9.31.8.en: * He appeared in His bodily form and gave Himself as a body, drawing to Himself the carnal, that He might first transform them into the likeness of the Word who became flesh, and then afterward into what He was before He became flesh.

9.32.0.en: Origen. "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me" [34].

9.32.1.en: * Who can take away the rod of God, that is, His divine wrath, so that man is no longer terrified of it? It is our Lord Jesus Christ, who laid our iniquity upon Himself, and brought us into the divine love, so that by His Holy Spirit we became sons of God, with boldness toward Him.

9.32.2.en: "Let him take his rod away from me" [34], for since He became incarnate and became like us, He does not strike us with the rod nor with fear, on condition that we flee to His grace and to faith, flee to Him who rose from the dead. The angel said to the women: [Fear not ye] (Mt 28:5, 10). And when He appeared to the disciples He used the same language again. In this sense Job continued: "Then would I speak, and not fear him" [35]. For He has done away with fear for us, and established the law of love (Mt 22:37-39). This is what John the Theologian wrote: [Perfect love casteth out our fear] (cf. 1 Jn 4:18).

9.32.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "Then would I speak, and not fear him."

9.33.0.en: "But it is not so with me" [35].

9.33.1.en: Through the Mediator we enter in to the Father with the boldness of sonship, enjoy His love, and rejoice in union with Him.

9.33.2.en: * Under the Law God held the rod, saying: [If a man does this or that, let him die the death](ه). But in His incarnation He took away His rod, showing the way of life by gentle means. For it was said to Him by the Psalmist: [Ride on and reign and rejoice, because of truth and meekness and righteousness](و). For He does not think to frighten as God, but dwells in our hearts as a loving Father. As Paul clearly teaches us: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Therefore it was fitting to add here: "Then would I speak, and not fear him" [35], for when the saint saw the Savior of the world coming in meekness, he did not wrap himself in fear, but by the grace of adoption ascended to love. John says: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear" (1 Jn 4:18). And Zacharias says: "That we, being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, might serve him" (Lk 1:74).

9.33.3.en: Fear has no power to raise us from the death of sin, but the grace of meekness poured out raises us to the throne of life. This was indicated by Elisha, for when he sent his servant with the staff, he did not at all bring life back to the dead boy. But when he came in person and stretched himself upon the dead body, and joined himself to its members, and walked to and fro, and breathed into the mouth of the dead body seven times, he restored it to the light of new life through the ministry of tenderness... So God, when He presented the terror of the Law by Moses, was like one who sent the staff by the servant. But when He came in His own person and stretched Himself in humility upon the dead body, He made Himself joined to the members of the dead body". Who, "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man..." (Phil 2:6-8).

9.33.4.en: He breathed into the dead body seven times, by declaring the divine grace, granting the Spirit of sevenfold grace to those cast down in the death of sin. After this he arose alive, in that boy whom the staff of terror could not raise, but who received life by the Spirit of love.

9.33.6.en: * Why are you afraid, O Christians?

9.33.7.en: Christ speaks: "It is I; be not afraid."

9.33.8.en: Why are you troubled by these things? Why are you afraid?

9.33.9.en: I told you beforehand that these things would surely happen... "It is I; be not afraid. Then they willingly received him into the ship."

9.33.10.en: When they knew Him and rejoiced, they were freed from their fears. "And immediately the ship was at the land whither they went." An end was found at the land, from the watery region to the solid region, from disturbance to steadiness, from the way to the goal.

9.33.11.en: St. Augustine. * It is God's will not to deliver you from fears, but to urge you to despise them, for this is greater than being delivered from them.

9.33.14.en: * Who is justified before You, O Holy One?

9.33.15.en: If You judge, it is You who are justified!

9.33.16.en: If You declare my sins, my grief is without measure.

9.33.17.en: If You bring a thousand accusations, I cannot answer with a word!

9.33.18.en: You are the searcher of hearts and reins; my thoughts and my hidden weaknesses are not hidden from You.

9.33.19.en: I confess to You that I am a sinner.

9.33.20.en: * I cannot stand before You in dispute, for You are Wisdom itself and Power.

9.33.21.en: Before You the firm mountains are moved, and they know it not.

9.33.22.en: Before You the proud souls collapse, and the human mountains melt like wax before the fire.

9.33.23.en: Let all pride within me be moved.

9.33.24.en: And let all corruption in my depths melt away.

9.33.25.en: And let Your holy mountains arise, Your steadfast word, in place of my proud, failing mountains!

9.33.26.en: * The Jews thought that they were the owners of the high mountains, since they received the Law, and from them came the fathers and the prophets.

9.33.27.en: These mountains were moved away from them, and You transferred them to us, that we may enjoy them in the Spirit and not the letter.

9.33.28.en: You unveiled to us the inner mysteries of the Law, and You declared to us the prophecies fulfilled by Your coming.

9.33.29.en: And You shone upon us with the truth in place of the shadows!

9.33.30.en: Glory to You, who set up Your mountains in our depths!

9.33.31.en: * How can I enter into judgment with You, O mighty Creator?

9.33.32.en: You command the sun and it does not rise, and the stars and they do not move.

9.33.33.en: Let the sun stand still, and my inner darkness appear; let the stars stop, that I may find no glimmer of inner light!

9.33.34.en: In place of the visible sun, rise upon me, O Sun of righteousness, for I need You, since I sit in darkness.

9.33.35.en: Shine upon me with the light of Your righteousness, and raise up from me a star that bears the splendor of Your glory.

9.33.36.en: Instead of justifying myself before You, let me possess You and be justified.

9.33.37.en: * How can I appear before You as in a court of justice, when You stretch out the heavens and walk on the heights of the sea?

9.33.38.en: Let a heaven arise from my earth, that I may become a dwelling for You.

9.33.39.en: Pass through the inside of my soul as over a raging sea.

9.33.40.en: Your presence silences the waves and calms the winds and the storms.

9.33.41.en: I am in need of the riches of Your grace, for You pass by me and I do not see You, You go by and I do not perceive You.

9.33.42.en: Who can say to the Creator, Why have You done so?

9.33.43.en: I keep silent in the midst of the storm, and await Your presence, for You are the Physician of my soul, who heal me of my many deadly wounds!

9.33.45.en: I want to hear Your voice!

9.33.46.en: * Why is my soul disturbed when the earth is given into the hand of the wicked?

9.33.47.en: Behold, the devil has become the ruler of this evil world!

9.33.48.en: Let him reign, but the earth will pass away, and he will descend into Hades!

9.33.49.en: Why does my soul groan, when You, the Holy One, became man!

9.33.50.en: The devil aimed the arrows of death at You, and did not realize that You are the resurrection and eternal life.

9.33.51.en: By Your own will You gave Your body over to death for a time.

9.33.52.en: That You might destroy death and kill it in its own house.

9.33.53.en: I no longer fear the wicked one, for he will no longer find in me an earth to receive.

9.33.54.en: You have turned my earth into heaven, so there is no place for the enemy of good within me!

9.33.55.en: * I look forward to my departure with joy and gladness of heart!

9.33.56.en: My life is counted as a ship on the sea, leaving no trace on the waters.

9.33.57.en: And I fly like an eagle in the sky, leaving no trace of my journey in the air.

9.33.58.en: By Your Holy Spirit I fly to You, and rest in the bosom of Your heavenly Father.

9.33.59.en: I boast of nothing but Your Cross and the riches of Your grace that covers my weaknesses and my evils!

9.33.60.en: * I will not justify myself! No, I have nothing with which to be justified.

9.33.62.en: You alone take away the enmity, and bring me into the bosom of Your Father.

9.33.63.en: You speak by Your blood, so I am filled with hope and love!

9.33.64.en: In You alone and through You I enjoy the eternal glories.
